arguments.name: Fights are about positions on an unknown line
arguments.conclusion: Every major political fight is an argument about where to sit on a line whose existence and mathematical structure the participants do not know.
arguments.speaker: David Lowe
premises: P1: Immigration, guns, abortion, healthcare, criminal justice, climate, AI, culture war, Trump, system rigging, left/right/libertarian disputes are all ongoing, unresolved fights (S005-S023).
P2: Each of these fights is an argument about where to sit on a line (S025).
P3: Nobody in the argument knows the line exists (S026).
P4: The line has a mathematical structure, a constraint making resolution impossible from inside, a repeating history, and exactly one exit off the line (S027-S030).

st1.quote: Every one of those fights is an argument about where to sit on a line.

st2.quote: The line has a mathematical structure. It has a constraint that makes resolution impossible from inside.

st6.quote: It has a history that shows the same pattern repeating across civilizations that never communicated.

or1.quote: Every one of those fights is an argument about where to sit on a line.
or1.why: No known prior work frames all political disputes as positions on an unknown mathematical line with a single off-line exit.

or2.quote: It has a history that shows the same pattern repeating across civilizations that never communicated.
or2.why: Claims a cross-civilizational repeating pattern as evidence, but no data is supplied.

or3.quote: The line has a mathematical structure.
or3.why: Connects political conflict to a mathematical constraint, a cross-domain bridge not made in standard political theory.

or4.quote: It has a constraint that makes resolution impossible from inside.
or4.why: Gestures at a formal constraint/model but no equation or structure is given.

arguments.weakest_link: P3/P4: the existence and mathematical structure of the 'line' is asserted with no evidence or formalization.
arguments.develop_next: Provide the actual mathematical structure of the line and a testable prediction of the repeating historical pattern.

arguments.name: Good and bad are structural properties
arguments.conclusion: Good and bad are structural properties of reality, as invariant as electric charge, not cultural opinions.
arguments.speaker: David Lowe
premises: P1: The document will show that good and bad are structural properties of reality (S040).
P2: These properties are as invariant as electric charge (S040).
P3: They are not cultural opinions that shift with the century (S040).

st1.quote: That good and bad are structural properties of reality, as invariant as electric charge — not cultural opinions that shift with the century.

st2.quote: That good and bad are structural properties of reality, as invariant as electric charge.

arguments.prior_art: Robert Adams, Finite and Infinite Goods (moral realism as resemblance to God), 1999

or1.quote: good and bad are structural properties of reality
or1.why: Moral realism is a well-worn position; the 'structural property' framing is a variant, not a new argument.

or2.why: Uses a physics analogy (electric charge) not standard in moral realism.

or3.why: Bridges physics invariance to moral ontology, a cross-domain move.

arguments.weakest_link: P1: the claim is only announced as something 'the document will show', with no supporting argument in this text.
arguments.develop_next: Supply the actual argument and evidence that moral properties are invariant in the way electric charge is.

arguments.name: No system can determine its own moral direction
arguments.conclusion: No system can determine its own moral direction from inside itself, and this is a proven mathematical result, not philosophy.
arguments.speaker: David Lowe
premises: P1: The document will show that no system can determine its own moral direction from inside itself (S042).
P2: This is mathematics, not philosophy (S042).
P3: It has been proven (S042).

st1.quote: That no system can determine its own moral direction from inside itself — this is mathematics, not philosophy, and it has been proven.

st2.quote: this is mathematics, not philosophy, and it has been proven.

arguments.prior_art: Kurt Gödel, incompleteness theorems, 1931 (often extended to self-reference limits)

or1.quote: no system can determine its own moral direction from inside itself
or1.why: A variant of the Gödelian self-reference limit applied to morality.

or3.why: Bridges formal mathematics to moral epistemology.

arguments.weakest_link: P3: 'it has been proven' cites no theorem, proof, or source.
arguments.develop_next: State the actual theorem and proof (or cite the formal result) that no system can determine its own moral direction.

arguments.name: External reference point must exist
arguments.conclusion: An external reference point must exist for the good/bad distinction to be meaningful, and such a reference point has maintained a continuous, accessible record throughout human history.
arguments.speaker: David Lowe
premises: P1: An external reference point must exist for the good/bad distinction to be meaningful (S044).
P2: Such a reference point has maintained a continuous, accessible record throughout human history (S044).

st1.quote: That an external reference point must exist for the distinction between good and bad to be meaningful — and that such a reference point has maintained a continuous, accessible record throughout human history.

st2.quote: An external reference point must exist for the distinction between good and bad to be meaningful.

arguments.prior_art: William Lane Craig, moral argument for God, 1979/1994

or1.quote: An external reference point must exist for the distinction between good and bad to be meaningful
or1.why: A variant of the standard moral argument for a divine ground.

or2.quote: such a reference point has maintained a continuous, accessible record throughout human history
or2.why: Adds a historical-record premise not standard in the moral argument.

or3.quote: a continuous, accessible record throughout human history
or3.why: Links moral grounding to a historical record, a mild cross-domain move.

arguments.weakest_link: P2: the claim of a continuous, accessible historical record of the reference point is asserted without evidence.
arguments.develop_next: Identify the record and show it is continuous and accessible, with sources.

P2: The sequence is money, government, education, reality-interpreters, moral language (S046).

st1.quote: That institutions get captured in a specific, documented, ordered sequence — money first, then government, then education, then the people who interpret reality for everyone else, then the moral language itself.

st2.quote: money first, then government, then education, then the people who interpret reality for everyone else, then the moral language itself.

or1.quote: institutions get captured in a specific, documented, ordered sequence

arguments.weakest_link: P1/P2: the ordered sequence is asserted as 'documented' but no documentation is given here.

arguments.name: Population sorts by connection to truth
arguments.conclusion: The population sorts into two classes over time, defined not by demographics but by whether their connection to truth runs through captured institutions or directly to the source.
arguments.speaker: David Lowe
premises: P1: The population sorts into two classes over time (S050).
P2: The sorting is defined by one structural feature: connection to truth via captured institutions or directly to the source (S050).
P3: It is not defined by any demographic variable (S050).

st1.quote: That the population sorts into two classes over time, defined not by any demographic variable but by one structural feature

st2.quote: whether their connection to truth runs through the captured institutions or directly to the source.

or1.quote: defined not by any demographic variable but by one structural feature
or1.why: A distinctive two-class sorting thesis not matching a known prior argument.

or3.quote: whether their connection to truth runs through the captured institutions or directly to the source
or3.why: Links institutional capture to epistemology of truth-access.

arguments.weakest_link: P1/P2: the two-class sorting is asserted with no data or criterion for measuring 'connection to truth'.

arguments.name: Communication technologies follow capture pattern
arguments.conclusion: Every communication technology in history follows the same pattern: a brief window where truth spreads, followed by institutional capture of the infrastructure.
arguments.speaker: David Lowe
premises: P1: Writing, printing press, radio, television, internet, and social media are communication technologies in history (S052).
P2: Each follows the same pattern: brief truth-spread window, then institutional capture of infrastructure (S052).

st1.quote: That every communication technology in history — writing, the printing press, radio, television, the internet, social media — follows the same pattern: a brief window where truth spreads, followed by institutional capture of the infrastructure.

st2.quote: a brief window where truth spreads, followed by institutional capture of the infrastructure.

or1.quote: every communication technology in history ... follows the same pattern

or2.quote: writing, the printing press, radio, television, the internet, social media

arguments.name: Justice and mercy cannot both be fully satisfied
arguments.conclusion: A mathematical constraint provable by algebra shows that justice and mercy cannot both be fully satisfied inside any closed system; someone always eats the deficit.
arguments.speaker: David Lowe
premises: P1: There is a mathematical constraint provable by algebra (S054).
P2: It shows justice and mercy cannot both be fully satisfied inside any closed system (S054).
P3: Someone always eats the deficit (S055).
P4: The only question is who, and whether they chose to (S056).

st1.quote: there is a mathematical constraint — provable by algebra — showing that justice and mercy cannot both be fully satisfied inside any closed system.

st2.quote: Someone always eats the deficit. The only question is who, and whether they chose to.

arguments.prior_art: Gustaf Aulén, Christus Victor, 1931 (atonement as necessity); Anselm, Cur Deus Homo, 1098

or1.quote: justice and mercy cannot both be fully satisfied inside any closed system
or1.why: A variant of the classic atonement-necessity argument, now cast as algebra.

or3.quote: a mathematical constraint — provable by algebra

or4.why: Claims a formalization but gives no equation.

arguments.weakest_link: P1/P2: the 'algebraic' constraint is asserted but never stated or proven.
